---
title: "Assessment and marking"
---

| Component | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Weekly coding exercises: ten best submissions | 20% |
| Midterm project proposal | 20% |
| Final research-design memo | 20% |
| Project presentation | 30% |
| Participation | 10% |

## Weekly coding exercises

The ten best submissions from the weekly tasks offered through the 18 November meeting count. There is no weekly coding task on 25 November, 2 December or 9 December. Each narrated screen recording is due by **5:00 p.m. Eastern on the Tuesday before the next class** unless the relevant weekly page states otherwise. Use the [recording instructions and coding videos folder](recording-and-submission.qmd).

In the recording, students run the complete block supplied on the week's Python page, explain the input and output of every operation, change one named input or parameter, and explain what the model return means for the week's methodological question. From Week 2, the normal route is a live call through OpenRouter or a supported local model; a supplied cached response may be used when access fails. Students are not graded for editing quality, code elegance or efficient abstraction.

A task is complete when the recording makes the student's understanding audible: the relevant Python values and types are identified, the model call and returned object are explained, the requested change is shown, one limit is stated and the connection to a reading is made. Weekly tasks do not receive numerical quality grades. Missing elements may be supplied within one week.

## Midterm project proposal

The proposal is released after Week 6 and is due at the end of Week 7: **Friday 23 October at 23:59 Eastern**. Submit it through the [Midterm project proposal page on NYU Brightspace](https://brightspace.nyu.edu/d2l/lms/dropbox/admin/folders_manage.d2l?ou=599622).

In 1,200–1,500 words, you set out a sociological question, locate it in a focused body of literature, specify the evidence and research design, and explain exactly where an LLM would enter the study. Include one concrete input → operation → expected output → researcher check, along with a validation plan, likely failures, ethical issues, the records you would preserve and the next steps toward the final project.

This is the first substantial version of the final project. It is not a Python test, and it does not require a completed empirical study or an exhaustive literature review.

## Final research-design memo

The final memo develops the midterm proposal into a complete design for an LLM-related sociological study. A minimal input/output trace or proof of concept is expected where feasible, but you are not required to complete a full empirical paper or obtain definitive findings.

Submit the memo before your individually scheduled meeting with the instructor on **2 December**. Submission details and meeting times will be circulated to the class. The memo should contain the sociological motivation, focused literature position, inferential target, data and sampling plan, proposed LLM workflow, prototype or trace where feasible, validation strategy, failure modes and ethics, reproducibility record, AI-use disclosure, and a brief account of how the design changed after the midterm.

The memo is assessed for sociological importance, fit between claim and design, transparent implementation, validation, substantive interpretation and reproducibility. Code sophistication is not an independent virtue.

## Project presentation

On **9 December**, present the research design developed in the memo. Each student has 10–12 minutes, followed by questions. The presentation should make the sociological problem, proposed evidence, role of the LLM, validation strategy and most consequential limitation clear. The presentation mark reflects the clarity and coherence of the argument, effective use of evidence or an inspectable trace, and the ability to explain and defend the design in discussion.

## Participation

Participation can take the form of a reading question, explanation of a code block, validation critique, project feedback or a short written contribution. Speaking frequency alone does not determine the mark.
